inputs.need:
I manage pharmacy services at a 350-bed community hospital. Our pharmacists cannot take a best possible medication history for every admission, so for two years our pharmacy technicians have taken histories in the emergency department and on the medical wards. They now want to take on discharge reconciliation too: comparing the discharge prescription with the admission history and the inpatient chart, and flagging discrepancies for the pharmacist. Before our pharmacy and therapeutics committee decides whether to extend the technicians' role to discharge, I want a scoping review of what is known about pharmacy technicians doing medication reconciliation at care transitions: which tasks they do, what training and supervision models exist, how accuracy has been measured, what outcomes have been reported, and what regulators or professional bodies allow.

I think a scoping review is right because the literature is probably scattered across settings, designs and countries, and we want a map rather than a pooled effect. We need to finish by the end of March so the committee can decide in April. One pharmacist can spend four hours a week on it, a pharmacy resident might join as a second reviewer if the residency director agrees, and we have access to the hospital library's databases. I would like the review to include reports from practice and professional organisations as well as journal articles. We are particularly interested in rural hospitals and in whether technicians' work changes what pharmacists do with their time.

records.title: Accuracy of medication histories taken by pharmacy technicians and pharmacists in the emergency department: a paired comparison
records.authors: Bamidele-Frost C, Nordgren-Sato E, Ruiz-Okafor L
records.abstract: For 240 adult admissions through one emergency department, a pharmacy technician and a pharmacist each took a best possible medication history, blind to each other. Against a reference history compiled by a second pharmacist, technicians recorded 91 percent of medications correctly and pharmacists 93 percent. Omissions of as-needed and over-the-counter medicines were the most common errors for both groups. Technicians took a median of 18 minutes per history and pharmacists 15 minutes. The study did not examine reconciliation at discharge or transfer.

records.title: Pharmacy technician-led discharge medication reconciliation on medical wards: discrepancies detected and pharmacist workload
records.abstract: On three medical wards, trained technicians compared discharge prescriptions with the admission medication history and the inpatient chart for 1,120 discharges over nine months, and referred discrepancies to a pharmacist. Technicians identified at least one unintentional discrepancy in 34 percent of discharges; pharmacists confirmed 88 percent of the discrepancies referred. Technicians spent a median of 11 minutes per discharge, and most referrals concerned omitted or duplicated medicines. Pharmacist time spent on discharge reconciliation fell by about 60 percent, and pharmacists reported more time for ward rounds. No patient outcomes were measured.

records.title: Training and supervision models for pharmacy technicians in medication reconciliation: a review of programme descriptions
records.authors: Grayson-Obi M, Laurent-Kimura T, Adjei-Sorensen P
records.abstract: We identified 46 published and unpublished descriptions of programmes that train pharmacy technicians to take medication histories or reconcile medications. Training ranged from a four-hour workshop to a 12-week accredited course, and 29 programmes required a competency assessment before independent practice. Supervision models included pharmacist review of every history, review of a sample, and review only of flagged discrepancies. Only 11 programmes described how competence was maintained over time, and discharge reconciliation was part of 9 programmes. Few programmes described how supervision was adapted for night or weekend work.

records.title: Scope of practice for pharmacy technicians in medication reconciliation: a comparison of regulatory frameworks
records.abstract: We compared regulations and professional guidance on pharmacy technicians' roles in medication reconciliation across 14 jurisdictions. All allowed regulated technicians to collect medication histories, but only 5 allowed technicians to compare lists and document discrepancies at discharge without a pharmacist present, and none allowed technicians to resolve discrepancies with prescribers. Requirements for registration and training differed widely. Some jurisdictions required a named supervising pharmacist on site, while others accepted remote supervision. The authors note that local policy must be checked against the current regulation, which changed in 4 jurisdictions during the study.

records.title: Pharmacy technicians in rural hospitals: roles, staffing and medication reconciliation coverage
records.abstract: We asked the pharmacy leads of 118 rural hospitals about technician roles and medication reconciliation coverage. Hospitals where technicians took medication histories reported histories for 78 percent of admissions, against 41 percent where only pharmacists did. Discharge reconciliation by technicians was reported by 12 hospitals. Leads cited limited pharmacist availability at weekends and the distance to supervising pharmacists as the main barriers. Responses were self-reported and not checked against records. The response rate was 61 percent, and hospitals without technicians were less likely to respond.

records.title: Readmissions after technician-supported discharge reconciliation: a before-after study
records.abstract: One hospital added technician-supported discharge reconciliation for medical patients and compared 30-day readmissions for 12 months before and 12 months after. Readmission fell from 14.2 to 13.1 percent, a change the authors describe as within the range of secular variation. Medication-related readmissions judged by a pharmacist fell from 2.9 to 2.1 percent. The comparison did not account for a new discharge summary template introduced in the same year. Pharmacists reviewed a tenth of technician reconciliations and agreed with 95 percent of them.

records.title: Medication reconciliation at care transitions: a map of outcome measures used in 150 evaluations
records.abstract: We catalogued the outcome measures used in 150 evaluations of medication reconciliation at admission, transfer or discharge. The most common measures were the number of unintentional discrepancies (71 percent of evaluations) and pharmacist-judged potential harm (38 percent); readmission was reported by 22 percent and patient-reported outcomes by 4 percent. Definitions of a discrepancy varied between evaluations, and only 18 percent described how outcome assessors were trained. Evaluations rarely stated who judged potential harm or whether they knew the intervention period. The authors propose a core set of outcomes for future evaluations.

response.synthesis: Seven records from the second recorded search, appraised at abstract level; the first search returned none. Technicians take admission histories with accuracy close to pharmacists', and one hospital reports technician-led discharge reconciliation that found discrepancies in a third of discharges and freed pharmacist time. Training and supervision models vary widely, regulators differ on whether technicians may document discharge discrepancies, and outcome definitions are inconsistent. Patient outcomes are rarely measured. The field is scattered, which suits a scoping review that charts tasks, supervision, measures and scope.
response.gradeRationale: Descriptive and before-after studies, programme descriptions and regulatory comparisons; low certainty for accuracy, very low for patient outcomes.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four claims with passages; certainty low; Scan now complete on retrieved records.

steps.note: Scan completes here because records were retrieved by a recorded event (G2), not because of the earlier model key. Certainty over seven inspected records (G1). Applied through the appraisal mapper (S13).

response.reading: Technician reconciliation spans three transitions (admission, transfer, discharge) and three layers that shape safety: what task the technician does, who supervises and how, and what the regulator allows. The retrieved evidence is densest for admission histories (claim c1), thin for discharge (claim c2), and bounded by jurisdiction-specific scope (claim c3). Outcomes are measured inconsistently (claim c4), so the review must chart definitions rather than compare numbers.

response.title: Pharmacy technicians in medication reconciliation at care transitions: a scoping review
response.abstract: Objective: to map what is known about pharmacy technicians performing medication reconciliation at admission, transfer and discharge. Design: scoping review following JBI guidance, reported with PRISMA-ScR. Sources: three bibliographic databases and professional and regulatory websites, English, from 2000. Results will be charted by task, supervision, measures, outcomes and scope.
response.introduction: Technicians take accurate admission histories in many hospitals, but their role at discharge, how they are supervised and what regulators allow are scattered across settings and jurisdictions.
response.methods: Searches were run by the hospital library; screening and charting used a form tested on the first seven retrieved records. The first recorded search returned no records and the second returned seven, both reported. Items not reported in sources were charted as not reported.
response.results: No charting has been done yet. The report will present the PRISMA-ScR flow diagram, an evidence map of tasks by transition, supervision models, outcome definitions and a scope table by jurisdiction.
response.discussion: The discussion will set out what the map means for the committee's decision on discharge reconciliation and where regulation, not evidence, is the limit.
response.limitations: English only; possible single-reviewer screening; grey literature may be incomplete.
response.conclusion: To be written after charting; it will describe the field and will not estimate effects.
